expansionNote: Authored from scratch (no prior question bank existed for this chapter beyond 5 hand-seeded placeholders). 40 questions across 11 learning objectives, targeting the same difficulty/bloom balance style as linear-equations and data-handling: conceptual/definitional recall, direct formula application, and multi-step reasoning (angle back-solving, hierarchy reasoning, property-distinguishing). Difficulty split: 15 Easy (37.5%), 17 Medium (42.5%), 8 Hard (20%) — close to Data Handling's easy-skew, reflecting that several objectives (polygon classification, shape-property recall) are foundational-recall by nature.

questions.prompt: What is a polygon?
questions.expectedAnswer: A simple closed figure made up entirely of line segments.
hints: Think about what a polygon's sides are made of — straight lines or curves?
It must also be closed and 'simple' (its boundary doesn't cross itself).

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Any closed shape, including ones with curved sides like a circle.
misconception.why: Students often use 'closed shape' as a shortcut for 'polygon' without checking that the sides are straight line segments.
misconception.remediationHint: A polygon's boundary is made only of straight line segments — a circle or any curved-boundary shape is not a polygon.

questions.prompt: A shape has 5 straight sides, but its boundary crosses itself once. Is it a polygon? Why or why not?
questions.expectedAnswer: No — a polygon must be a simple closed curve, meaning its boundary must not cross itself.
hints: A polygon must be 'simple' — think about what that means for the boundary.
If the sides cross each other, the figure is not simple.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Yes, because it still has straight sides and is closed.
misconception.why: Students often check only 'straight sides + closed' and forget the 'simple' (non-self-intersecting) requirement.
misconception.remediationHint: Having straight sides isn't enough — the boundary must also not cross itself.

questions.prompt: What is true of every interior angle of a convex polygon?
questions.expectedAnswer: Each interior angle is less than 180°.
hints: Compare this to a concave polygon, which has at least one 'caved-in' vertex.
At a caved-in vertex the interior angle is more than 180° — convex polygons never have this.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: All angles must be exactly 90° in a convex polygon.
misconception.why: Confusing 'convex' with 'rectangular' or 'right-angled' shapes.
misconception.remediationHint: Convex only requires every angle to be under 180° — it says nothing about being exactly 90°.

questions.prompt: A polygon has one interior angle measuring 200°. Is this polygon convex or concave?
questions.expectedAnswer: Concave
hints: Compare 200° to the convex-polygon rule (every interior angle less than 180°).
Since 200° is greater than 180°, this vertex is 'caved in'.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Convex, because most polygons look convex by default.
misconception.why: Students often assume a typical-looking polygon is automatically convex without checking every angle.
misconception.remediationHint: Check every interior angle — even one angle over 180° makes the whole polygon concave.

questions.prompt: A hexagon has interior angles 100°, 110°, 120°, 130°, 140°, and 260°. Is this hexagon convex? Explain.
questions.expectedAnswer: No, it is concave, because the 260° angle is greater than 180°.
hints: Convexity depends on checking each individual angle, not the overall shape of the figure.
Look for any single angle greater than 180°.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Convex, since only one angle looks unusual and the rest seem normal.
misconception.why: Students judge convexity by overall appearance rather than checking every angle individually.
misconception.remediationHint: Even a single interior angle over 180° makes the entire polygon concave.

questions.prompt: What makes a polygon 'regular'?
questions.expectedAnswer: All its sides are equal in length and all its angles are equal in measure.
hints: A regular polygon must satisfy two conditions at once — think about sides and angles separately.
Equal sides alone is not enough if the angles differ.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: A regular polygon just needs all sides equal.
misconception.why: Students often stop at the side condition and forget angles must also be equal.
misconception.remediationHint: Both conditions — equal sides and equal angles — must hold together for a polygon to be regular.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal in length, but its angles are 80°, 100°, 80°, 100°. Is it a regular polygon?
questions.expectedAnswer: No, because its angles are not all equal.
hints: Regularity needs both equal sides AND equal angles.
Here the sides are equal — now check the angles.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Yes, since all the sides are equal.
misconception.why: Students often treat equal sides alone as sufficient for 'regular' (this shape is a rhombus, not a square).
misconception.remediationHint: A regular polygon needs equal sides AND equal angles — a rhombus like this one satisfies only the first condition.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral?
hints: Use the formula (n − 2) × 180° with n = 4 for a quadrilateral.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 180°, confusing it with a triangle's angle sum.
misconception.why: The triangle's 180° angle sum is memorized first and sometimes misapplied to any polygon.
misconception.remediationHint: Each shape has its own angle sum — a quadrilateral's is 360°, found via (4 − 2) × 180°.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon (5 sides)?
hints: Use the formula (n − 2) × 180° with n = 5.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 450°, from an arithmetic slip while applying the formula.
misconception.why: Arithmetic slips are common when applying a two-step formula quickly.
misconception.remediationHint: Compute (n − 2) first, then multiply that whole result by 180°.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of an octagon (8 sides)?
hints: Use the formula (n − 2) × 180° with n = 8.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 1440°, by using n × 180° instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
misconception.why: Students often forget to subtract 2 before multiplying.
misconception.remediationHint: Always subtract 2 from the number of sides first, then multiply by 180°.

questions.prompt: A polygon's interior angles sum to 1260°. How many sides does it have?
hints: Set (n − 2) × 180° = 1260° and solve for n.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 7, from dividing 1260 by 180 and stopping there.
misconception.why: Students solve for (n − 2) correctly but forget to add back the 2 to get n.
misconception.remediationHint: Dividing gives you (n − 2), not n — add 2 back to find the actual number of sides.

questions.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95°, and 100°. Find the fourth angle.
hints: The four angles of a quadrilateral must add up to 360°.
Add the three known angles, then subtract that total from 360°.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 195°, from only subtracting two of the three given angles.
misconception.why: Arithmetic slip — forgetting to add all three known angles before subtracting from 360°.
misconception.remediationHint: Add all three known angles together first, then subtract that total from 360°.

questions.prompt: In a quadrilateral, three angles are equal to 90° each, and the fourth is unknown. Find the fourth angle.
hints: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.
Subtract 3 × 90° from 360°.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 180°, guessing a 'nicer' round number instead of computing.
misconception.why: Guessing a familiar angle value rather than doing the subtraction.
misconception.remediationHint: Subtract the sum of the three known angles from 360° exactly — don't guess.

questions.prompt: In a pentagon, four angles are 100°, 110°, 120°, and 95°. Find the fifth angle.
hints: The sum of the interior angles of a pentagon is 540° (use (n − 2) × 180° with n = 5).
Add the four known angles and subtract that total from 540°.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 360°, applying the quadrilateral's angle sum instead of the pentagon's.
misconception.why: 360° is the most memorized angle-sum fact and gets applied automatically without checking the number of sides.
misconception.remediationHint: This shape has 5 sides, so its interior angle sum is 540°, not 360°.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral's angles are in the ratio 2:3:4:6. Find all four angles.
hints: The four angles must sum to 360°. Let the angles be 2x, 3x, 4x, 6x.
Solve 2x + 3x + 4x + 6x = 360° for x, then multiply each ratio term by x.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Treating the ratio numbers themselves (2°, 3°, 4°, 6°) as the actual angles.
misconception.why: Students sometimes skip finding the scale factor and treat ratio terms as literal angle measures.
misconception.remediationHint: The ratio numbers must be scaled up by a common factor x so that all four angles add to 360° — find x first.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon, taken one at each vertex, in order?
hints: This is true no matter how many sides the polygon has.
It's always a full turn — 360°.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: It depends on the number of sides.
misconception.why: Since the interior angle sum depends on n, students assume the exterior sum must too.
misconception.remediationHint: Unlike the interior angle sum, the exterior angle sum is always 360°, regardless of the number of sides.

questions.prompt: A regular polygon has 9 sides. Find the measure of each exterior angle.
hints: For a regular polygon, each exterior angle = 360° ÷ number of sides.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 9°, from dividing 9 by 360 instead of 360 by 9.
misconception.why: Students sometimes invert the division.
misconception.remediationHint: It's always 360° divided by the number of sides, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 24°. How many sides does the polygon have?
hints: Use: number of sides = 360° ÷ each exterior angle.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 24 sides, by dividing 24 by 360 instead of 360 by 24.
misconception.why: Same inversion error as with computing a single exterior angle.
misconception.remediationHint: Number of sides = 360° ÷ each exterior angle — divide the total by the angle, not the angle by the total.

questions.prompt: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 156°. How many sides does it have?
hints: Find the exterior angle first: interior + exterior = 180° at each vertex.
180° − 156° = 24°, then use 360° ÷ exterior angle to find the number of sides.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: 360° ÷ 156°, using the given interior angle directly without converting it first.
misconception.why: Students try to shortcut straight to 360° ÷ (given angle) without checking whether the given angle is interior or exterior.
misconception.remediationHint: This is an interior angle — first subtract it from 180° to get the exterior angle, then use 360° ÷ exterior angle.

questions.prompt: A regular polygon has an interior angle that is 5 times its exterior angle. Find the number of sides.
hints: Let the exterior angle be x, so the interior angle is 5x. Use interior + exterior = 180°.
x + 5x = 180° gives x = 30°; then use 360° ÷ x to find the number of sides.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Guessing a plausible number of sides without solving x + 5x = 180° first.
misconception.why: Skipping the algebra step and guessing a round number instead.
misconception.remediationHint: Set exterior = x, interior = 5x, solve x + 5x = 180° for x first, then use 360° ÷ x.

questions.prompt: What do you call a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides?
questions.expectedAnswer: Trapezium
hints: It has one pair of parallel sides, called the bases, and one pair of non-parallel sides, called the legs.
In some regions this shape is also called a trapezoid.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Parallelogram, since it has parallel sides.
misconception.why: Students associate 'parallel sides' generally with parallelogram, without checking how many pairs.
misconception.remediationHint: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides; a shape with only one pair is a trapezium.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Can it be called a trapezium?
questions.expectedAnswer: No, because a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides — this shape is a parallelogram.
hints: Check the trapezium's defining condition carefully — how many pairs of sides must be parallel?
A shape with both pairs parallel belongs to a different quadrilateral family.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Yes, since it has at least one pair of parallel sides.
misconception.why: Students sometimes use 'at least one' instead of the 'exactly one' definition taught for trapezium in this course, confusing it with parallelogram.
misconception.remediationHint: In this course, a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides; a shape with both pairs parallel is classified as a parallelogram instead.

questions.prompt: In a trapezium, the two parallel sides are called the ______, and the two non-parallel sides are called the ______.
questions.expectedAnswer: bases, legs
hints: Think of the trapezium as sitting on its parallel sides.
The slanted connecting sides have their own separate name.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Swapping the two terms — calling the parallel sides 'legs' and the slanted sides 'bases'.
misconception.why: The two terms sound interchangeable without a clear anchor.
misconception.remediationHint: The bases are the parallel sides (like the base a shape rests on); the legs are the slanted connecting sides.

questions.prompt: What is true about the sides of a kite?
questions.expectedAnswer: It has two distinct pairs of adjacent sides that are equal in length.
hints: Look at which sides are equal — are they opposite each other, or next to each other?
In a kite, the equal sides are adjacent (next to each other), not opposite.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Opposite sides are equal, like a parallelogram.
misconception.why: Overgeneralizing the parallelogram's opposite-sides-equal rule to all quadrilaterals with some equal sides.
misconception.remediationHint: In a kite, it's adjacent (neighboring) sides that come in equal pairs, not opposite ones.

questions.prompt: What is true about the diagonals of a kite?
questions.expectedAnswer: They intersect at right angles, and one diagonal bisects the other.
hints: Think about how a kite's diagonals cross — at what angle?
Only one of the two diagonals is cut exactly in half by the other.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Both diagonals bisect each other, like in a parallelogram.
misconception.why: Students often over-generalize the parallelogram's 'diagonals bisect each other' rule to every quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals.
misconception.remediationHint: In a kite, only one diagonal is bisected by the other — not both, unlike a parallelogram.

questions.prompt: A kite has sides of length 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm, and 8 cm. How must these sides be arranged around the kite?
questions.expectedAnswer: The two 5 cm sides must be adjacent to each other, and the two 8 cm sides must be adjacent to each other.
hints: A kite's equal sides come in two adjacent pairs, not opposite pairs.
Arrange the sides so each pair of equal length shares a common vertex.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Arranging the sides alternately as 5, 8, 5, 8 around the kite.
misconception.why: Students expect equal sides to alternate, as in a parallelogram, rather than being grouped adjacently.
misconception.remediationHint: A kite's equal-length sides must be next to each other in pairs (5, 5, 8, 8 in order), not alternating.

questions.prompt: What is true about the opposite sides of a parallelogram?
questions.expectedAnswer: They are parallel and equal in length.
hints: Check both properties — direction and length.
Both pairs of opposite sides share both properties.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Only equal, or only parallel, not both.
misconception.why: Students sometimes remember only one half of the two-part property.
misconception.remediationHint: Both properties hold together: opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel AND equal.

questions.prompt: What is true about the opposite angles of a parallelogram?
questions.expectedAnswer: They are equal.
hints: Compare angles that are diagonally across from each other.
Each pair of opposite angles has the same measure.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: They are supplementary, confusing them with adjacent angles.
misconception.why: Mixing up which angle pair — opposite vs. adjacent — gets which rule.
misconception.remediationHint: Opposite angles are equal; it's the adjacent angles that are supplementary.

questions.prompt: What is true about two adjacent (consecutive) angles of a parallelogram?
questions.expectedAnswer: They are supplementary (they add up to 180°).
hints: Adjacent angles share a side.
Their measures always add up to a straight angle.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: They are equal, confusing them with opposite angles.
misconception.why: Same opposite/adjacent mix-up as the opposite-angles question, in the other direction.
misconception.remediationHint: Adjacent angles add up to 180° (supplementary); it's the opposite pair that's equal.

questions.prompt: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A = 70°. Find angle B (adjacent to A) and angle C (opposite to A).
questions.expectedAnswer: Angle B = 110°, Angle C = 70°
hints: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram are supplementary.
Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Angle B = 70°, treating all angles as equal.
misconception.why: Students sometimes assume a parallelogram behaves like a rectangle with all equal angles.
misconception.remediationHint: Only opposite angles are equal in a general parallelogram — adjacent angles are supplementary, not equal.

questions.prompt: What is true about the diagonals of a parallelogram?
questions.expectedAnswer: They bisect each other.
hints: Think about where the diagonals cross.
The point where they cross divides each diagonal into two equal halves.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: They are equal in length, confusing this with a rectangle's diagonal property.
misconception.why: Overextending the rectangle's 'equal diagonals' rule to all parallelograms.
misconception.remediationHint: All parallelogram diagonals bisect each other, but they're only guaranteed equal in length for a rectangle.

questions.prompt: In parallelogram PQRS, the diagonals intersect at O. If PO = 6 cm, find OR, and explain why.
questions.expectedAnswer: OR = 6 cm, because the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so O is the midpoint of diagonal PR.
hints: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other — what does that mean for PO and OR specifically?
PO and OR are the two halves of the same diagonal PR.
No calculation needed — apply the bisection property directly to PO and OR.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Can't be determined without more information.
misconception.why: Students sometimes don't realize the bisection property alone answers the question, and look for a missing side length instead.
misconception.remediationHint: The bisection property alone tells you PO = OR directly — no other measurement is needed.

questions.prompt: What extra property does a rhombus have that a general parallelogram does not?
questions.expectedAnswer: All four sides are equal in length.
hints: A rhombus is a parallelogram with one extra condition on its sides.
Compare the side lengths of a rhombus to a 'plain' parallelogram.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: All angles equal 90°, confusing it with a rectangle.
misconception.why: Mixing up which special parallelogram gets the side condition and which gets the angle condition.
misconception.remediationHint: A rhombus's extra condition is about sides (all equal); the angle condition (all 90°) belongs to a rectangle.

questions.prompt: What extra property does a rectangle have that a general parallelogram does not?
questions.expectedAnswer: All four angles are 90°.
hints: A rectangle is a parallelogram with one extra condition on its angles.
Every angle in a rectangle measures the same amount — what is it?

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: All sides equal, confusing it with a rhombus.
misconception.why: Same rhombus/rectangle mix-up, in the other direction.
misconception.remediationHint: A rectangle's extra condition is about angles (all 90°); the side condition (all equal) belongs to a rhombus.

questions.prompt: How are the diagonals of a rectangle different from the diagonals of a general parallelogram?
questions.expectedAnswer: A rectangle's diagonals are equal in length (as well as bisecting each other).
hints: Both shapes' diagonals bisect each other — that's not the difference.
Compare the lengths of the two diagonals in each shape.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: A rectangle's diagonals bisect each other but a parallelogram's don't.
misconception.why: Students sometimes assume the 'bisect each other' property is exclusive to rectangles, when it's actually shared by all parallelograms.
misconception.remediationHint: Diagonals bisecting each other is true for every parallelogram — a rectangle's distinguishing diagonal property is that they're also equal in length.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal AND all four angles equal to 90°. What is the most specific name for this shape?
questions.expectedAnswer: Square
hints: This shape satisfies the rhombus condition (all sides equal) and the rectangle condition (all angles 90°) at the same time.
A shape that is both a rhombus and a rectangle has one specific name.
Combining both special conditions at once gives the most specific quadrilateral name of all.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Rhombus, stopping at the side condition without checking the angles too.
misconception.why: Students recognize one matching condition and stop, without checking whether a more specific name applies.
misconception.remediationHint: Satisfying both the rhombus condition and the rectangle condition at once makes it a square — the more specific name.

questions.prompt: In a square, what is true about the diagonals that is NOT true of a rhombus that isn't a square?
questions.expectedAnswer: The diagonals are equal in length.
hints: A square is both a rhombus and a rectangle — combine what you know about each.
Rhombus diagonals bisect at right angles; rectangle diagonals are equal — a square has both, but a non-square rhombus is missing one.
List the rhombus's diagonal properties, then the rectangle's, and find the one only in the rectangle's list.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, thinking this is unique to squares.
misconception.why: Perpendicular bisecting diagonals are already true for every rhombus, not just squares — the genuinely new property is about length.
misconception.remediationHint: Perpendicular bisecting diagonals are true for any rhombus; a square's distinguishing extra property is that its diagonals are also equal in length.

questions.prompt: Is every square a rectangle? Is every rectangle a square? Explain.
questions.expectedAnswer: Every square is a rectangle (it has all angles 90°), but not every rectangle is a square (a rectangle need not have all sides equal).
hints: Check the rectangle's defining condition — does a square satisfy it?
Check the square's defining condition (all sides equal) — does every rectangle satisfy that too?

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Every rectangle is also a square.
misconception.why: Reversing the direction of the hierarchy — assuming the relationship works both ways.
misconception.remediationHint: The 'is-a' relationship only goes one way here: square → rectangle, not rectangle → square.

questions.prompt: Is every rhombus a parallelogram? Is every parallelogram a rhombus? Explain.
questions.expectedAnswer: Every rhombus is a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel and equal), but not every parallelogram is a rhombus (its sides need not all be equal).
hints: Check whether a rhombus satisfies the parallelogram's defining properties.
Check whether a general parallelogram automatically has all four sides equal.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Every parallelogram is also a rhombus.
misconception.why: Same reversed-hierarchy error as with squares and rectangles.
misconception.remediationHint: Rhombus → parallelogram is one-directional; a general parallelogram doesn't automatically have all sides equal.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral is a square. List every other quadrilateral name from this chapter that also correctly describes it.
questions.expectedAnswer: Rectangle, rhombus, and parallelogram
hints: Work outward from the square: what two shapes combine to make a square?
Both of those shapes are themselves special cases of an even more general quadrilateral — name that one too.
Square is a rectangle; square is a rhombus; both rectangle and rhombus are parallelograms.

misconception.commonWrongAnswer: Only 'rectangle' and 'rhombus', forgetting parallelogram.
misconception.why: Students stop one level up the hierarchy and forget that both rectangle and rhombus are themselves parallelograms.
misconception.remediationHint: Follow the hierarchy all the way up — since a square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and both of those are parallelograms, 'parallelogram' also correctly describes it.
